description: Every night you dream for about two hours. Most of those dreams are gone the moment you wake. Here is what science understands about the mystery today.

hero.hook: You spend about six years of your life dreaming. And you forget nearly all of it.

blocks.text: Every night you spend about **two hours** dreaming. Over a lifetime that adds up to nearly **six years**. Yet within seconds of waking, most of those stories vanish.

Scientists still disagree about the “why.” But they know more and more about **when** we dream, and what the brain is doing at the time: reorganizing memories, testing out scenarios and digesting emotions.

Sleep is not a clean break. It moves in **cycles** of about **90 minutes**, several times a night. In each cycle the brain passes through different phases: light sleep, deep sleep that repairs the body, then one very strange phase.

blocks.caption: During REM sleep, the eyes move under the eyelids

blocks.text: That phase is called [[REM sleep]]. The brain is almost as active as when you are awake, but the body is held still by [[Muscle atonia]]. This is where long, story-like dreams mostly come from. The paralysis stops you from physically acting out what you dream.
We dream **4 to 6 times** a night and forget about **95%** of it within ten minutes of waking. If you remember a dream, it is usually because you woke up during it or right after.

sections.title: Sleep is not the lights going out

blocks.text: **Freud** believed dreams mostly revealed hidden desires. Today researchers prefer more concrete explanations, based on **brain imaging**, techniques that show the brain at work. Dreaming lights up the **limbic system** above all, the set of deep structures tied to emotion.

blocks.caption: While you dream, the brain is working: emotions, images, memories

blocks.text: Three big ideas dominate. First: **sorting memory**, keeping what is useful and letting the rest go. Second: **rehearsing danger** in a world where nothing can really hurt you. Third: **digesting emotions**. During a dream the brain revisits intense moments with less **norepinephrine**, a neurotransmitter linked to stress and alertness.
To store a memory for the long term, the brain needs certain chemicals. During REM sleep, the level of norepinephrine drops. The result: the dream is held in a very fragile memory.
The moment you open your eyes, light, sound and the thoughts of the day crush that fragile trace. The best way to keep it? Write the dream down **right away**, before you even move.
Before color television, few people said they dreamed in color. Today most of us do. Even the texture of our dreams follows what we look at all day.

Sometimes you realize **that you are dreaming** while you are still asleep. That is a **lucid dream**. An area of the brain tied to logic and self-reflection, the **prefrontal cortex**, switches partly back on.

Some people can then steer the scenery or turn a nightmare around. Researchers are even studying the effect to help athletes rehearse movements in their heads, or to treat nightmares that keep coming back.

We dream above all during [[REM sleep]], a phase when the brain is active and the body is still. Dreaming probably helps us manage memory and emotion, even though we forget nearly all of it on waking.
